title: Roll the dice again
text: Board games were supposed to be dead, {{1}} by screens. Instead they are booming: hundreds of new titles {{2}} each year, cafes dedicated to playing them {{3}} in cities from Seoul to Sao Paulo, and sales have grown steadily for two decades. The {{4}} lies in what screens cannot offer. A board game is a reason for people to sit at the same table for hours, talking, teasing and reading each other's faces — the screen scatters the room's attention; the board gathers it. The other change is {{5}}: in the 1990s, German designers pioneered games of short rules and long strategy, with no player {{6}} before the end and nothing decided until the last turn. Titles like Catan and Carcassonne proved that a game could be deep without being complicated, and a generation of designers has been {{7}} the formula ever since: hidden roles, worker placement, decks that evolve as you play. The phone, ironically, ended up as the board game's ally — companion apps handle the bookkeeping, and online communities {{8}} rules disputes within minutes. What cannot be digitised is the oldest technology of all: sitting round a table, together, taking turns.

gaps.explanation: 'supposed to be dead, killed by screens' — the cause of the supposed death; cajole = persuade gently.
'new titles appear each year' — come into existence; 'appeal' needs 'to', and titles cannot applaud or apply.
'cafes multiply in cities' — grow rapidly in number; mortify = embarrass deeply.
'the appeal lies in what screens cannot offer' — the attraction; appendix = a section at the back of a book, apparel = clothing.
'the other change is design' — the way games are built; desert = dry land or to abandon, dessert = sweet course.
'no player eliminated before the end' — removed from the game; elaborate = add detail to.
'designers have been refining the formula' — polishing it; refrain takes 'from', refund is for money.
'communities resolve rules disputes' — settle them; revolt = rise up against, revolve = go round.
